conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re adjusting since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way.

Today I’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply 10 questions that help us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up during the first year postpartum, and it includes one question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Nothing you say leaves this room unless you or your baby’s safety is at immediate risk.

We’ll go one question at a time. For each item, just tell me how you’ve felt in the past seven days—no right or wrong answers, and it’s okay if your answer changes day-to-day. Ready to start?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

[sighs gently, eyes down for a second]

Honestly… most of the time I can still laugh. My partner did make me chuckle at one of his silly voices yesterday. But it feels muted, like I have to push myself to really enjoy it. Before the baby I’d have been in stitches, and now it’s more like “oh, that’s funny” and then I move on.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… like I said, I can still laugh, but it’s not the same full-hearted feeling I used to have.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[wrings hands a little]

I do look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over tomorrow so I can take a walk—but the excitement feels kind of flat. Before the baby, I’d be counting the hours; now it’s more “I guess that’ll be nice.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet for a second, then nods]

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Like when he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. and I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding him right, or I missed some cue. My head knows babies just cry, but I still hear this little voice saying, “You should’ve figured it out by now.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[exhales slowly]

Sometimes I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly feel this wave of worry—like, is he breathing okay, is that weird little rash something serious? I check him, everything’s fine, and I can calm myself down pretty quick, but the anxious feeling still comes out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[shifts in seat, hugging the baby blanket on my lap]

A couple of times—mostly at night when the house is quiet—I’ll get this sudden tightness in my chest, like something bad is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes in a minute or two if I do the breathing the nurse showed me, but it still catches me off-guard.
Things have been getting on top of me

[shoulders rise in a small shrug]

Some days, yeah. Like yesterday—he wouldn’t nap, laundry was piled up, and I still hadn’t eaten lunch by three. For a minute I felt swallowed by it, but I took a breath, put him in the carrier, and got through the chores bit by bit. I manage, it’s just… harder than it used to be.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[shakes head slowly]

Not really. I’m sad off and on, but it hasn’t messed with my sleep—once I finally get to bed I’m out. It’s just falling asleep that’s tricky some nights because my mind keeps running through the day or I jump at every little sound he makes.
I have felt sad or miserable

[draws a slow breath, eyes on the floor]

Yeah… I’d say I feel that way a good chunk of the day. It’s not constant, but it’s like there’s this heavy blanket that settles over me. I can still smile when the baby coos or when my partner brings me tea, yet the sadness keeps drifting back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quiet nod, voice a little thick]

Twice this week. Once when he wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch, and again yesterday when I dropped a plate and it shattered. Both times the tears just came, lasted a few minutes, then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes widening]

No—never. I feel overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of him.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has dulled since your baby arrived: laughter feels <quote>muted</quote>, anticipated outings now feel <quote>flat</quote>, and a <quote>heavy blanket</quote> of sadness settles over you most days. While you can still soothe and care for your little one, waves of worry, sudden chest tightness, and tearful moments catch you off-guard, and you often blame yourself for every hiccup in his routine.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished anticipation and describes excitement as "flat," matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a couple of times" and describes specific instances, aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden waves of worry multiple times daily without clear cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "a good chunk of the day" with sadness "drifting back in," matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 14 meets the ≥14 threshold indicating probable peripartum depression requiring urgent assessment. Core symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: daily depressed mood and diminished interest/anhedonia for most of the day, plus guilt, crying, and functional difficulty despite intact caregiving. Co-occurring <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> are common in postpartum presentations. Patient denies self-harm, so immediate safety risk is low, yet score mandates prompt follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Request concurrent screening with <med>PHQ-9</med> and <med>GAD-7</med> for baseline severity
3. Discuss individual or group <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> and, if indicated, antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding
4. Encourage 15-20 min outdoor daylight walks and acceptance of help with night feeds to consolidate 4 hr sleep blocks
5. Provide 24-hr crisis line numbers and schedule re-screen in two weeks to track symptom trend
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approximately 2–3 wks after delivery (per chart)  
Date: ___  
Screener: ___

Presenting Symptoms / Behaviors endorsed
- Persistent low mood (“heavy blanket”), crying spells ×2 this week  
- Marked reduction in pleasure/enthusiasm (laughter “not full-hearted,” anticipatory enjoyment “flat”)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care (“should have figured it out”)  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety/worry with somatic tension (chest tightness, “wave of worry”)  
- Brief nocturnal panic episodes (≤2 min) relieved by breathing techniques  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; difficulty initiating sleep due to racing thoughts  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (clearly stated “never”)  
- No current impairment in full overnight sleep once asleep; no appetite concerns voiced

Patterns / Clustering
- Consistent with mixed mood–anxiety presentation: low affect plus near-daily anxious arousal  
- Function intact (self/soothes, completes chores, utilizes support) but tasks require “extra effort”  
- No psychotic or safety red flags; protective factors (partner, mother support) present

Screening significance
- Meets threshold items for possible minor–moderate postpartum depression (sadness, anhedonia, tearfulness, guilt)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms exceed baseline baby-related concerns (frequency, physical symptoms)  
- Risk factors: primiparous, sleep deprivation, self-criticism; mitigated by insight, social support, no self-harm intent

Overall screening impression
Moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms within postpartum context; safety risk currently absent.  
Recommend: formal EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7; consider expedited referral for perinatal mental health evaluation and psychoeducation.
